extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and policymakers interested in online disinformation, social media manipulation, and Chinese internet practices
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizing and evaluating the phenomenon of paid online posting operations (internet water armies) — their definition, types, tactics, organization, legality, detection methods, and scale. Useful for researchers, journalists, or practitioners studying astroturfing and social-media manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Internet water army'
rubrics_metrics.description: An Internet water army (网络水军) is a group of users who are paid to post online comments with vested interest on Chinese language websites; they post news, comments, gossip and disinformation on platforms like Weibo, WeChat and Taobao.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets the baseline for identifying such operations: paid posting with vested interests, coordinated activity across Chinese-language platforms; contrasts with organic users.

rubrics_metrics.name: Features of paid posting
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid posting involves thousands of individuals and posters using different online IDs; the content is usually well-prepared and there is a quality control team to check whether the postings meet the customer's standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include large volumes of posts, multiple distinct accounts controlled by the operation, professionally composed copy, and explicit quality-control/validation steps for payments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of Internet water armies
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three types: (1) those who voluntarily spread posts promoting social justice; (2) those hired by the government or state-owned companies to promote CCP propaganda; and (3) those who work for private companies (PR firms) to pursue private interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify an operation by its client/mission (voluntary activism vs. state-sponsored propaganda vs. private PR/marketing). Different types imply different content targets and constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tactics / customer services offered
rubrics_metrics.description: Three customer services listed: promotion of a specific product, company, person or message; slandering an adversary or their products or services; and helping delete negative or unfavorable posts or news articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating campaigns, look for these tactical goals (promotion, smear, deletion). Examples include leaving positive reviews, posting negative reviews about competitors, or offering content removal/cleanup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market pricing and service tiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Pricing varies from 'basic zombie' for less than 5 yuan per 1,000 (Taobao market) to 'A-level zombie' with realistic profiles for 120 yuan per 5,000; price depends on content complexity and desired authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pricing and tiering indicate sophistication: very low-cost mass accounts vs. higher-cost accounts with photos, self-descriptions and followers. Use pricing data to infer scale and quality of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational structure of operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical teams include a project manager; a trainer team that plans schedules, distributes shared user IDs, and maintains quality control; a posters team (often college students/unemployed) paid per validated post; a resources team that registers/collects user IDs; and a PR team that maintains client relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizational signatures (presence of trainers, dedicated account-resourcing, validation/payment mechanics) can differentiate organized water armies from ad-hoc brigading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivations and economic drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Clients: online marketing firms, celebrity agencies, entertainment companies seeking positive reviews or inflated followers, businesses seeking to smear rivals; Participants: migrants, housewives, students seeking part-time income — many earn more than a thousand yuan per month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding motivations helps predict which sectors are targeted (entertainment, e‑commerce) and why supply of posters persists (low entry barriers, steady income).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship to government '50 Cent Party' and distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The '50 Cent Party' refers specifically to paid posters employed by the Chinese government/CCP to spread propaganda and control public opinion; it is narrower than 'internet water army' and typically avoids touching sensitive issues while pushing pro-CCP messaging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish state-sponsored campaigns (which have political aims and content constraints) from private commercial operations when attributing motive and likely content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal risks and legitimacy concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations can run afoul of laws (e.g., China's cyber defamation law, revisions to Tort Liability Law), face cease-and-desist from foreign companies, and have led to arrests, prosecutions, account closures, and regulatory crackdowns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing operations, consider legal exposure (defamation, fake transactions, privacy violations). Past legal actions and regulatory changes are evidence of state response and potential client/firm risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection indicators (behavioral patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unusual patterns include many negative comments or replies from newly registered user IDs that are seldom used afterwards; followers who never interact (e.g., ~17% of followers on top microblogs never interacted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral red flags: sudden bursts from new accounts, one-off posts followed by dormancy, lack of reciprocal interaction; use these heuristics to flag likely paid accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection methods and algorithms
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly detection approaches include a Dirichlet process mixture model (DPMM)-based GSP algorithm and sequential pattern mining to analyze user behavior; case studies used large datasets and found promising performance for automated detection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical detection combines probabilistic clustering (DPMM), sequential pattern mining, and features like account registration age, posting frequency, and interaction patterns. Empirical validation on labeled datasets is recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale and impact metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported scale examples: as of 2008, around 40 percent of trending hashtags on Weibo were created by Internet water armies; companies can earn millions of yuan in short periods; studies estimated hundreds of millions of fabricated comments by state actors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prevalence statistics (share of trending topics, transaction volumes, estimated fabricated comment counts) to assess societal impact and prioritize detection/mitigation efforts.
